clue.text: Good to stay in after hours, far from fully fit

blocks.note: H is the standard abbreviation for hours
read as 'a bit able': only somewhat capable, so far from fully fit

explanation.surface: Someone told to stay in after hours to recover, still far from fully fit.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay comes first: H, then the phrase A BIT ABLE. 'Good to stay in' is the definition, as a house might be.
explanation.definitionFit: A dwelling that is fit to live in, offering decent shelter, can be called a suitable place for residents.

clue.text: Put up with dated tool

blocks.note: to hack something is to put up with it, as in 'can't hack it'
if you saw someone you dated them, went out with them

explanation.surface: Someone tolerates an old-fashioned implement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dated' looks like an adjective meaning old, but it is the verb: to see someone is to date them, so 'dated' is SAW.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a fine-toothed saw in a frame, used for cutting metal, so it is one kind of workshop implement.

clue.text: Rely on drunk for financing

blocks.note: to bank on something is to rely on it
as in 'rolling drunk', very drunk

explanation.surface: Someone depends on an alcoholic to fund them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rely on' needs its preposition: BANK on. 'Rolling' alone stands for drunk from the phrase 'rolling drunk'.
explanation.definitionFit: To supply someone with money for a venture is to fund or back it, which is what paying the costs means.

clue.text: New leaves elevated a huge area of forest

indicators.note: something that leaves goes away, so that letter is dropped from the rest
in a down clue, raising letters up the column makes them read bottom to top

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for new; it is the letter removed
taken as written
giant as an adjective means huge

explanation.surface: Fresh foliage raised up across an enormous stretch of woodland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New leaves' sounds like fresh foliage, but it means the letter N departs: A GIANT loses N to become A GIAT, which then reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The taiga is the vast belt of coniferous woodland across Siberia and northern Canada, south of the tundra.

clue.text: Aussie famous for being in Republican villain’s clothing

indicators.note: clothing wraps around a body, so one piece is dressed in the other

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican
a bad man, a baddie, is a villain

explanation.surface: An Australian known for hiding inside a Republican villain's outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman who is 'in' is batting; Don Bradman, the great Australian batsman, was famous for staying in. The 's in 'villain's' reads as 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Donald Bradman, Australia's legendary batsman, averaged 99.94 in Tests, so he was celebrated for long innings at the crease.

clue.text: Every now and then, dialled up priest

indicators.note: something done every now and then happens at intervals, so only every other letter is kept
in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom of the column to the top

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Occasionally someone phones a clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dialled up' looks like a phone call; 'up' belongs to the reversal, not to 'dialled'.
explanation.definitionFit: Eli is the Old Testament high priest at Shiloh who raised the young Samuel, a favourite crossword cleric.

clue.text: New business set shoppers back

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the letters are read from right to left

blocks.note: to set something down is to put it
to shop someone is to inform on them, and informers are rats

explanation.surface: A fledgling firm that cost customers dearly, setting them back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shoppers' are not customers: to shop someone is British slang for informing on them to the police, so shoppers are RATS.
explanation.definitionFit: A newly founded company, especially a small tech firm seeking growth, is the usual sense of this hyphenated term.

clue.text: Sort of sailor cap drunk’s put on

blocks.note: a sot is a habitual drunk
OS is an ordinary seaman
the peak is the stiff brim at the front of a cap

explanation.surface: A type of seaman's hat that a drunk has put on his head.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'put on' means placed above, so the drunk's letters go on top of the sailor and the cap.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are hedges admitting the words are not quite literal, in a manner of speaking or loosely put.

clue.text: Face up to what’s to be done about fungus

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: an act is a deed, something done
the cep is the edible porcini mushroom

explanation.surface: Confronting what must be done about a fungal problem.
explanation.walkthrough: CEP is a crossword favourite for a mushroom, the French name for the porcini.
explanation.definitionFit: To face up to an unwelcome situation is to acknowledge and tolerate it rather than resist, the same as resigning yourself to it.

clue.text: People are carefully considering including small piece of commentary

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: people in general, as in 'they say'
to think it all over is to consider it carefully
S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A crowd weighing up a short extract from a broadcaster's remarks.
explanation.walkthrough: THEY THINK IT ALL OVER takes in S to become the famous line. Kenneth Wolstenholme said it on BBC television as fans ran onto the pitch at the end of the 1966 World Cup final, adding 'it is now'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is among the best-known lines in English sports broadcasting, spoken live by the BBC football commentator in 1966.

clue.text: Unusually chirpy winner at the end, describing expensive victory?

indicators.note: unusual means out of the normal order, so the letters are arranged differently
the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: taken as written, ready for rearranging
the final letter

explanation.surface: A champion is oddly cheerful at the finish after a costly win.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as descriptive rather than a synonym: the adjective is usually found before the word 'victory'.
explanation.definitionFit: King Pyrrhus of Epirus beat Rome but lost so many soldiers that the triumph ruined him; a win won at ruinous cost carries his name.

clue.text: Not the sole hiker?

blocks.note: first meaning: the part of a shoe above the sole
second meaning: one who hikes, or raises, prices or a total, read whimsically

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hiker' pretends to be a walker, whose boots fit the shoe picture, but here it is one who hikes up a figure.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoe has a sole underneath and a leather top above it; and someone who raises something up could jokingly be named for that action.

clue.text: Lubricant heartlessly applied to fish is not refined

indicators.note: without a heart means the central letter is taken out

blocks.note: UNGUENT, an ointment, with its middle letter removed
the eel is the crossword's commonest fish

explanation.surface: Smearing grease on fish is uncouth.
explanation.walkthrough: An unguent is a soothing ointment; the seven letters lose the central U.
explanation.definitionFit: Genteel means polite and respectable, so its negative describes coarse, unpolished manners lacking social graces.

clue.text: Levy for ownership of image consultancy ruined Tory expat

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked and broken up, so these letters are rebuilt in a new order

blocks.note: PR, public relations, manages image
taken as written, ready for rearranging

explanation.surface: A spin-doctoring firm has wrecked a Conservative living abroad, with a tax on his holdings in the background.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Image consultancy' sounds like a real business, but it only supplies the two letters of PR.
explanation.definitionFit: Councils and governments charge owners annually on land and buildings they hold, so the charge is a duty on possession of real estate.

clue.text: Teacher turning up on our side for a laugh

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning upwards means reading the letters from the bottom

blocks.note: pupils call a male teacher sir
our side is us, as in 'us and them'

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster switching to the pupils' side just for fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' in a down clue puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for a grin or chuckle, kept in English medicine in 'risus sardonicus', the fixed grimace of tetanus.

clue.text: Putting one’s own away in jail: note one sounding furious!

indicators.note: something sounding like a word is heard as it, though spelt otherwise

blocks.note: the can is slang for prison
N is short for note, and I is the Roman numeral one
to go ballistic is to become furious; the spelling follows the sound

explanation.surface: Locking up one's own people in prison, with a note from an inmate who is raging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting away' means eating, as in putting away a big meal, so putting one's own away is eating your own kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Eating members of your own species is the literal sense; 'putting away' is the informal phrase for consuming food greedily.

clue.text: Shocking, say, Number Ten confronting America

blocks.note: eg, for example, is what 'say' means
a reg is a vehicle registration number
I and O look like the digits 1 and 0
the US is America

explanation.surface: Something scandalous, such as Downing Street squaring up to the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number Ten' looks like the Prime Minister's home at 10 Downing Street, but it splits: a car's registration number, then the two letters that look like the digits 1 and 0.
explanation.definitionFit: The word now means outstandingly bad or flagrant, as in an outrageous error, though it once meant remarkably good.

clue.text: Missile on singular curved trajectory that can wound

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the noun: something that can wound

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another comes after it, so this piece is written last

blocks.note: S is the grammar abbreviation for singular
an arc is a curved path
an ASM is an air-to-surface missile

explanation.surface: A rocket on a curved flight path that can do harm.
explanation.walkthrough: The obvious missile abbreviation is SAM, surface-to-air, but the letters need its air-to-surface cousin. The definition is what the remark does: cutting words hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: Mocking irony aimed to hurt is notorious for stinging its target, so it is something capable of injuring feelings.

clue.text: Pitch needs grass, stupid!

definitions.note: an adjective used here as a term of address, standing for the noun

blocks.note: to pitch something is to toss it
grass and pot are both slang for cannabis

explanation.surface: An exasperated groundsman insists a cricket pitch needs grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' and 'grass' both look like the sports field; one is the verb throw and the other is the drug.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally a drunkard, the word is British slang for a fool, so it serves as an insult like 'idiot' shouted at someone.

clue.text: Fictional biography adapted poorly to life’s rhythm

indicators.note: an adapted thing is altered to suit, so the letters are refashioned

blocks.note: taken as written, ready for rearranging

explanation.surface: A made-up life story was badly fitted to the rhythm of real life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fictional biography' is precise: the novel is the invented life of a shopkeeper told as if it were a history.
explanation.definitionFit: H G Wells's 1910 comic novel follows a downtrodden draper through his life, framed as the account of one man's career.

clue.text: Husband gets passionate in suspenders

blocks.note: H is short for husband
to anger, intransitively, is to grow heated, to get worked up

explanation.surface: A husband grows amorous when he sees stockings and garters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passionate' suggests desire, but the passion is rage: he angers. Suspenders, in British English, hold up stockings, though here they are simply things that suspend.
explanation.definitionFit: Hooks or frames that hold things up so they hang are devices for suspension, so the two nouns name the same function.

clue.text: Civil engineering tip for grateful new aldermen

indicators.note: engineering is building or contriving, so the letters are constructed into a fresh order
a tip is an extreme end, so only the end letter is kept

blocks.note: the final letter
taken as written, ready for rearranging

explanation.surface: A thank-you gift on the subject of civil engineering for newly appointed councillors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Civil engineering' reads as one phrase, but the definition is 'Civil' alone and 'engineering' begins the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Being polite and courteous, showing good manners to others, is exactly what civil behaviour amounts to.

clue.text: Huge weight other than a stone may be lifted

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting raises letters so they read bottom to top

blocks.note: other than means not
taken as written
a precious stone is a gem

explanation.surface: Something enormously heavy, other than a stone, might be raised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stone' tempts as a unit of weight beside 'Huge weight', but it is a GEM.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit of a million tons, used chiefly for the explosive power of nuclear weapons, so a vast mass.

clue.text: Victorian wedding party take trips across river

indicators.note: something that trips stumbles and falls in a muddle, so the letters are jumbled
to go across something is to straddle it, so one piece spans the other

blocks.note: taken as written, ready for rearranging
the Itchen is a river in Hampshire, England

explanation.surface: A wedding reception in the reign of Queen Victoria, with guests taking excursions over a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victorian' is not the 19th century but the Australian state of Victoria. The river flows through Winchester and Southampton in Hampshire.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australia and New Zealand a bride-to-be's friends hold a pre-wedding gathering where they give her household utensils; it is that region's bridal shower.

clue.text: Inherited revolutionary skills in javelin, cycling

indicators.note: a revolution turns things right round, so the letters run the other way
cycling moves round in a loop, so the first letter goes round to the end
in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: arts are skills, as in the arts of war
a lance is a long spear, like a javelin

explanation.surface: Talent for throwing the javelin and riding a bike runs in the family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' looks like the sport beside 'javelin', but it moves the L of LANCE to the back, giving ANCEL, which then holds STRA.
explanation.definitionFit: Something handed down from forebears through the generations, such as a family seat, is passed on by descent.

clue.text: Going places? Yes, heading off for launches

indicators.note: with its head off, a word loses its first letter

blocks.note: 'going' as a euphemism for using the toilet; loos are toilets
the word without its first letter

explanation.surface: Travelling? Yes, setting off to get a boat into the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going places' sounds like travel, but a loo, British for toilet, is where you go when you need to go.
explanation.definitionFit: Archers loose arrows and armies loose missiles, so the verb means to fire or set free, the same as sending them off.

clue.text: Keep hold of fish, previously caught

blocks.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
the ling is a long fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: An angler hangs on to a fish that was hooked earlier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Previously' puts the letter for caught before the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: To grip tightly and refuse to let go is to retain a grasp, the meaning of the verb with or without 'to'.

clue.text: Nothing to stop rascal taking a year’s holiday abroad

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a gap, so one piece fills the middle of another

blocks.note: a cad is a dishonourable man, a rascal
nada is Spanish for nothing, used in English slang
taken as written
Y is short for year

explanation.surface: A scoundrel who takes a year off to travel is told he gets nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: For a British setter, a national day across the Atlantic is a holiday abroad; the 's of 'year's' is just the possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Canada's national day on 1 July marks Confederation in 1867, a public festival celebrated across that country overseas.

clue.text: Stop-go skill at hockey?

blocks.note: to stick is to stop moving, to jam
a machine that goes is one that works

explanation.surface: Is the ability to keep stopping and starting a talent in hockey?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stop-go' looks like one hyphenated term for a jerky rhythm, but it splits into two verbs.
explanation.definitionFit: Hockey players control the ball with a stick, so their handling and dribbling ability is named after the stick.

clue.text: “Like a slow dance?” — timid second officer’s opening

indicators.note: opening something up makes room within it for other letters

blocks.note: shy means timid
a mo is a moment, a second
OC is officer commanding

explanation.surface: A shy second lieutenant opens a dance with a hesitant question about slow dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after 'officer' reads as 'has': the timid piece has an opening, and the second and officer go into it.
explanation.definitionFit: A slow dance invites couples to hold each other close and kiss, so the dance is romantic and cuddly in that informal sense.

clue.text: Wise using force mostly to contain it

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
to contain is to hold within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: the police force, without its final letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sensible approach to using force, mostly to keep something in check.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force' here is a police force, cut short before the pronoun goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means shrewd and prudent, judicious in conduct, as in 'it would not be politic to complain'.

clue.text: After weathering the op, Reg has left hospital ward

indicators.note: weathering wears and changes a surface, so the letters are reshaped
whatever has left is gone, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
H is the map abbreviation for hospital; it is the letter removed

explanation.surface: Having come through his operation, Reg has been discharged from the hospital ward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ward' is not the hospital room the surface suggests but a person under someone's protection.
explanation.definitionFit: A protégé is someone guided and sponsored by a patron, as a ward is a young person placed under a guardian's care.

clue.text: Concierge to hand old-fashioned empty pot back

indicators.note: an empty word has lost its insides, so only the outer letters remain
going back means travelling the opposite way, so the letters read right to left

blocks.note: nigh means near, close to hand
retro styles imitate the past
the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A hotel doorman is asked to pass over an old empty pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pot back' tempts you to reverse the whole pot to TOP; only its emptied shell, joined to the old-fashioned piece, is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A hotel employee on duty through the dark hours who handles guests and the front desk does the job of a hall porter or concierge.

clue.text: Some verse of Frost’s recited

indicators.note: reciting is saying words aloud to an audience, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: rime is hoar frost, the white crystals on grass on a cold morning

explanation.surface: A few lines by the poet Robert Frost read out loud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frost' looks like the American poet, which fits 'verse', but it is frozen dew.
explanation.definitionFit: Short poems with matching end sounds, nursery jingles and the like, are pieces of poetry in the simplest sense.

clue.text: Argument and fights after pressure to provide viewing accessories

indicators.note: one thing after another follows it, so this piece is written second

blocks.note: a set-to is a quarrel or scrap
P is the physics symbol for pressure
to box is to fight with fists

explanation.surface: Rows and scuffles break out after someone is pushed to hand over the binoculars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Argument' looks like a reasoned case, but here it is a squabble.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the decoder units sitting on or near a television that receive cable or satellite channels, add-ons that let you watch.

clue.text: Establishment of relations with family member, not quite 50

indicators.note: not quite all means one short, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a sibling, a brother, without his final letter
L is the Roman numeral for 50

explanation.surface: Founding a family connection with a sibling who is nearly fifty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relations' looks like family, which the brother encourages, but it means sexual relations, and the establishment is a business premises.
explanation.definitionFit: A house where sex is sold is a commercial premises where intimate encounters take place, a cheeky reading of 'relations'.

clue.text: Add contrary alternative, as one does summing up?

indicators.note: an alternative is another version, so the letters are set in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written, ready for rearranging

explanation.surface: Someone told to add a contradicting option while giving a summary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Summing up' suggests a conclusion, but it means doing sums: in old-fashioned column arithmetic you set down the units and carry the tens to the next column.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes the schoolroom routine of written addition, noting a digit and moving the overflow along; it also names a limping gait.

clue.text: Pass battle scene where Pole tangled with the army

indicators.note: something tangled is knotted into a mess, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written, ready for rearranging
taken as written, ready for rearranging

explanation.surface: A battlefield where a Polish soldier clashed with the army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass' is not a verb but a mountain pass, and the definition runs on to 'battle scene'.
explanation.definitionFit: This narrow coastal pass in Greece is where Leonidas and his 300 Spartans held off the Persians in 480 BC.

clue.text: Alarmist medic, no good, entering second profession

indicators.note: to enter is to go inside, so these letters are put within another piece

blocks.note: S is short for second
a career is a profession
MO is a medical officer
NG is the abbreviation for no good

explanation.surface: A panicky doctor, useless at medicine, takes up another line of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second profession' reads as a second career, but 'second' contributes only its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who spreads frightening rumours and stirs up public panic is a doom-monger, the noun sense of the word.

clue.text: Fool, moreover joker, hard to take revenge on

blocks.note: a get is British dialect for an idiot, a variant of git
even, in the sense of 'indeed, and what's more'
a wit is a joker
H for hard, as on pencils

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard to' reads as 'difficult to', but 'hard' only gives its letter and 'to' joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To pay someone back for a wrong and square accounts is to retaliate, the idiomatic sense of evening the score.

clue.text: Film going into personal record on food intake

indicators.note: going into something means entering it, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: a diary is a personal daily record
ET is Spielberg's 1982 film about an alien

explanation.surface: Writing up a movie in a personal log of what one has eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an adjectival phrase: 'on food intake' means concerning it, as in dietary advice.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means relating to diet, the food and drink regularly consumed, so it describes matters concerning eating.

clue.text: State of old pit, alight and cracking up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the letters read from the bottom

blocks.note: an abyss is a bottomless pit
a fire that is in is still burning, alight
A1, written AI, means first-rate, cracking

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracking up' suggests collapse; 'cracking' is British slang for excellent. 'State' means a country, not a condition.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the former name for Ethiopia, the ancient East African empire, so it is a nation from history.

clue.text: Make too much of old potato served in relish?

indicators.note: food served in a dish sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: O is short for old
relish as gusto or zest
alu, or aloo, is the Hindi word for potato, familiar from Indian menus

explanation.walkthrough: 'Relish' is not a condiment here but zest; the potato is the one in aloo gobi.

clue.text: Confirmed boxer’s wearing very old hat

Muhammad Ali, the boxer
old hat means out of date

clue.text: Where to stay in Brighton after golf?

second meaning: in the NATO phonetic alphabet, the word for H follows Golf for G

clue.text: Fetching parent of 27 for Children’s Corporation

clue.text: At risk of retribution? What might a good penalty be?

clue.text: Appearing too smart repeatedly, not exactly what’s needed for purchase

clue.text: Be bursting with joy, close to you for a second

the final letter

clue.text: In a month’s time, Society coming up with reason

clue.text: Lots of courses teaching religion, history and science just starting

history is the past
the first letter

explanation.surface: A college offers many courses in religion, history and fledgling science.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Courses' looks like academic subjects, matching the teaching surface, but they are courses of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Meals, especially formal ones served as a succession of dishes, are made up of several courses.

clue.text: Note someone paid for copy

blocks.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale
a pro, a professional, is paid to play

explanation.surface: A musical note that someone was paid to produce a duplicate of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' could be a banknote, which suits 'paid', but it is the musical note.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for reproduction, it means a replica, especially of antique furniture or a printed image.

clue.text: Record returns, having subject to steal from

indicators.note: something that returns comes back the way it went, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: an LP is a long-playing record
under means subject to, as in under orders

explanation.surface: Sales figures come back, and a subject is accused of theft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record returns' sounds like a record profit or a tax return; it is a vinyl album turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: To plunder a place is to loot or rob it violently, stripping it of goods.

clue.text: Preferred source of learning: a thing to be cultivated

blocks.note: a pet subject is a favourite one
a uni, university, is a place of learning
taken as written

explanation.surface: A favourite university course teaches something worth developing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cultivated' suggests a refined mind, matching the learning surface, but it means grown in a garden.
explanation.definitionFit: This trumpet-flowered annual is grown in beds and hanging baskets, a plant raised by gardeners.

clue.text: Rear displayed by drag performer?

blocks.note: first meaning: to rise high, to soar above
second meaning: one who tows, drags something along behind

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drag performer' suggests a drag queen and 'Rear' a backside; one meaning is the verb to loom up, the other a vehicle pulling a load.
explanation.definitionFit: A cliff can loom high above you, and a lorry that hauls a caravan is one that pulls, the two senses of the word.

clue.text: Substandard work of setter, maybe, young and new, crossing line

indicators.note: crossing something cuts through its middle, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: the young of a setter, a gundog, is a puppy
L is short for line
novel means new

explanation.surface: A poor piece by the crossword setter, perhaps young and inexperienced, crossing the line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' looks like the crossword compiler, which suits 'work', but it is the dog breed.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheap sensational fiction printed on rough wood-pulp paper is the classic example of low-quality writing.

clue.text: Pigment transformed a unit with time

indicators.note: to be transformed is to change form, so the letters take a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written, ready for rearranging

explanation.surface: A colouring agent altered a unit over the years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A unit with time' reads like a measurement, which suits a science surface, but it is simply the letters to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: This bright opaque white colour made from titanium dioxide is the standard white in artists' paints.

clue.text: Meat roll is revolting

indicators.note: revolving or overturning, so the letters are turned to read backwards

blocks.note: a bun is a bread roll

explanation.surface: A disgusting meat-filled roll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meat' is not food but the essence of an argument, and 'revolting' means rebelling, turning over.
explanation.definitionFit: The central point or core of an issue, 'the meat of the matter', is its essential gist.

clue.text: Fine blossom, eg azalea, pruned

indicators.note: pruning cuts away the outer growth, leaving an inner section to be read

blocks.note: found across the end of the flower word, the abbreviation and the start of the shrub

explanation.surface: A lovely bloom such as an azalea, cut back by the gardener.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' looks like an adjective, but it is the Italian musical direction FINE, marking where a piece ends.
explanation.definitionFit: The last letter of the Greek alphabet stands for the end of anything, as in 'alpha and omega', just as 'fine' marks a score's close.

clue.text: Whiskey you had, days earlier, with not a drop to be seen!

definitions.text: with not a drop to be seen!

indicators.note: what comes earlier is placed before, so this piece is written first

blocks.note: D is short for days
rye is American whiskey
ye'd is old-style 'you had'

explanation.surface: A drinker finishes the whiskey days before, so there isn't a drop left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not a drop' suggests empty bottles, but the drops are tears.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who sheds no tears at a sad moment has no teardrops visible, the literal sense of the compound.

clue.text: Men hiding in tree: one had a flower

indicators.note: something hiding in a place is concealed inside it

blocks.note: the beech is a tree
OR, other ranks, are soldiers who are not officers
I'd is 'I had', with I as one

explanation.surface: Soldiers lurking in a tree; one of them picked a bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One had' is the pronoun I plus the contraction for 'had'.
explanation.definitionFit: A European wild orchid whose lip mimics a bumblebee to attract pollinators, so it is a wildflower species.
